source.title: A survey of equivariant map algebras with open problems

accepted.question_text: Let X be an affine scheme with coordinate algebra A, let a be a finite-dimensional algebra, and let an algebraic group Γ act completely reducibly on both A and a by automorphisms. For the resulting equivariant map algebra M(X,a)^Γ, classify the irreducible finite-dimensional representations when Γ is allowed to be more general than a finite group.

evidence.quote: (a) More general groups Γ. Instead of a finite group Γ, one can consider, for instance, an algebraic group acting completely reducibly on A and a. The first step in the study of the resulting EMAs would be to classify their irreducible finite- dimensional representations.

accepted.question_text: Develop the representation theory of equivariant map algebras M(X,g)^Γ when the target algebra g is allowed to be much more general than the finite-dimensional Lie or associative cases already studied, including infinite-dimensional Lie targets such as Kac-Moody or Heisenberg algebras and non-Lie targets such as alternative or Jordan algebras, with special emphasis on describing their finite-dimensional representations whenever representations are well defined.

evidence.quote: (b) More general targets. There are many possible choices for the “target” alge- bra g for which the resulting EMA has not been studied. Even in the setting of Lie algebras, one could consider g to be, for instance, a Kac-Moody algebra (see [ERF] for the untwisted multiloop case) or some other well-studied infinite-dimensional Lie algebra, such as the Heisenberg algebra.

In fact, one can study the representation theory of any EMA for which the target is an algebra with well-defined representations. For example, it would be natural to consider the finite-dimensional representations in the case of alternative algebras or Jordan algebras.

accepted.question_text: Generalize equivariant map superalgebras by allowing the target to be any finite-dimensional simple Lie superalgebra, replacing the commutative coordinate algebra A by a supercommutative algebra so that X becomes a superscheme, and replacing Γ by a Z2-graded group; then determine the resulting representation theory in this broader super setting.

evidence.quote: (c) Superschemes and superalgebras. The equivariant map superalgebra setting of [Sav] can be naturally generalized. First, one can consider more general Lie superalgebras for the target g. For example, one could take any finite-dimensional simple Lie superalgebra (not just basic classical ones). Furthermore, one can replace A by a supercommutative algebra (in other words, let X be a superscheme) and Γ by a Z2 -graded group.

accepted.question_text: Replace the algebraic framework of equivariant map algebras by an analytic one: for a Banach manifold X, a Banach algebra a, and an action of Γ by automorphisms, develop the theory and representation theory of algebras of equivariant differentiable maps X → a.

evidence.quote: (d) Analytic setting. Another interesting problem is to replace the algebraic setting by an analytic one. For example, let X be a Banach manifold, a a Banach algebra and consider equivariant differentiable maps X → a.

accepted.question_text: For equivariant map algebras M(X,a)^Γ, determine classification criteria and invariants for the isomorphism problem by extending known results for loop algebras and certain two-variable multiloop algebras to the full multiloop setting and then to more general equivariant map algebras.

evidence.quote: 4.2.1. Isomorphism problem. Characterizing EMAs up to isomorphism is one of the fundamental problems in the theory of EMAs.
It is therefore natural, though likely difficult, to try to generalize the results of both papers [ABP] and [GP07] to the multiloop case and beyond that to more general EMAs.

accepted.question_text: Determine the automorphism groups of equivariant map algebras M(X,a)^Γ in general, extending the partial descriptions already known in special untwisted, twisted-loop, multiloop, Lie, and Lie-superalgebra cases.

evidence.quote: 4.2.2. Automorphisms. Related to the problem of characterizing EMAs up to isomorphism, is the question of determining the automorphism groups of EMAs.

accepted.question_text: When a is an associative algebra and M = M(X,a)^Γ, go beyond the classification of irreducible finite-dimensional M-modules and describe all indecomposable finite-dimensional modules, together with the block decomposition of the corresponding module category.

evidence.quote: 4.2.3. Indecomposable modules. The classification of the irreducible objects in the category of finite-dimensional modules of M for an associative a in Theorem 2.1 is only a first step towards a complete understanding of the category. Ideally, one would like to describe all of the indecomposable finite-dimensional modules and understand the block decomposition of this category.

accepted.question_text: If a is an associative bialgebra and M = M(X,a)^Γ, understand the multi-orbit evaluation representations that arise from the comultiplication on a, including their construction, classification, and structural properties.

evidence.quote: 4.2.4. Associative bialgebras. In the case that a is an associative bialgebra, one can naturally define multi-orbit evaluation representations using the comultiplica- tion on a. It would be interesting to understand these representations.

accepted.question_text: For an equivariant map Lie algebra M = M(X,g)^Γ, compute the higher Ext groups between finite-dimensional M-modules, explain how these Ext groups interact with both the representation theory of g and the geometry of X, and determine how the global dimension of the category of finite-dimensional M-modules is governed by that geometry.

evidence.quote: (a) Higher extensions. Only the first Ext groups are calculated in [NS], where it is shown that these groups are related to both the representation theory of the target g and the geometry of the scheme X (see, for instance, Proposition 3.5, which involves the tangent space). It is natural to try to compute higher Ext groups. One would expect a rich interplay between these groups and the geometry of the scheme X. It would be particularly interesting to see how the global dimension of the category of finite-dimensional modules is related to this geometry.

accepted.question_text: Extend the theory of global and local Weyl modules from currently understood cases to more general equivariant map algebras, including determining lengths, dimensions, and characters of local Weyl modules, and extending BGG reciprocity to this broader EMA setting.

evidence.quote: (b) Weyl modules. The study of (global and local) Weyl modules for EMAs is an active area of research. In particular, one would like to extend the results on the lengths, dimensions and characters of the local Weyl modules (see [CP01, BN04, CL06, CM04, FL07, Nak01, Nao12]) to the setting of more arbitrary EMAs (see [FMSa] for the definitions of global and local Weyl modules in this setting). It is also natural to try to extend the notion of BGG reciprocity described in [BCM12, BBC+ ] to a more general EMA setting (see [BBC+ , Rem. 2.7]).

accepted.question_text: Develop representation-theoretic categories for equivariant map algebras beyond finite-dimensional modules, including analogues of category O, categories of integrable highest-weight representations, categories of quasifinite representations with finite-dimensional weight spaces, and other suitable infinite-dimensional module categories.

evidence.quote: (c) Possibly infinite-dimensional representations. Much of the current focus in the study of the representation theory of arbitrary EMAs has been on the category of finite-dimensional representations. However, in specific cases (most importantly, the loop and current algebras) more general categories of representations have been studied.

It would be interesting to study analogous categories in the more arbitrary EMA setting. For example, one could consider the category of integrable highest weight rep- resentations, the category of quasifinite representations (i.e. representations with finite-dimensional weight spaces) or appropriate generalizations of category O.

accepted.question_text: Assume g is semisimple and M = M(X,g)^Γ. Describe the first cohomology group H1(M,V) for a general M-module V, extending the partial results already known for some equivariant map algebras and locally finite modules; in particular, clarify this cohomology for the adjoint module Mad, where H1(M,Mad) = Der_k(M) / IDer(M).

evidence.quote: 4.3.2. Cohomology. Assume g is semisimple. The formulas for ExtM (V1 , V2 ) proven in [NS] have a cohomological interpretation since ExtM (V1 , V2 ) ≃ H1(M, Homk(V1 , V2)). One can therefore expect that it should be possible to describe the first cohomol- ogy group H1 (M, V ) for a general M-module V . For some equivariant map alge- bras M, including multiloop algebras, and locally-finite M-modules, this is done in [NP]. A particular instance of this question is the adjoint module Mad , for which H1 (M, Mad ) = Derk (M)/ IDer(M).

accepted.question_text: Determine the homology groups H_*(M,V) for equivariant map Lie algebras M and M-modules V, including the structural consequences for the abelianization H0(M,Mad) = M / [M,M] and for identifying perfect equivariant map algebras.

evidence.quote: A related problem is to determine the homology groups H∗ (M, V ). Some re- sults on H0 (M, Mad ) = M/[M, M] are contained in [NSS12] and [NS], see for example Lemmas 6.1 and 6.10 of [NS] describing classes of perfect equivariant map

algebras. The interest in perfect equivariant map algebras comes from Theorem 3.2 which indicates that these algebras have a simpler representation theory. A second reason is that perfect Lie algebras have universal central extensions, as discussed in Section 4.3.3 below.

accepted.question_text: For a perfect equivariant map Lie algebra M = (g ⊗ A)^Γ, understand its central extensions, especially the universal central extension uce(M), and determine when the universal central extension of the fixed-point algebra agrees with the fixed points of the universal central extension of the untwisted algebra, namely when uce((g ⊗ A)^Γ) is naturally isomorphic to uce(g ⊗ A)^Γ.

evidence.quote: 4.3.3. Central extensions. Central extensions of Lie algebras often have a sim- pler representation theory, the affine Kac-Moody Lie algebras being a case in point. It is therefore of interest to understand central extensions of equivariant map alge- bras M, preferably the universal central extension uce(M) of a perfect M.

Generalizing the example of twisted loop algebras, one would like to relate the universal central extension of a perfect equivariant map algebra (g ⊗ A)Γ to the well-understood universal central extension uce(g ⊗ A). Observe that the action of Γ on g ⊗ A uniquely lifts to an action on uce(g ⊗ A). The formula one is aiming for is then very natural: uce((g ⊗ A)Γ) ≃ uce(g ⊗ A)Γ.
